messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tama is a 63-year-old airline pilot, married and living in Honolulu, who served as a helicopter pilot during the Vietnam War. In 1970, his Huey was hit by ground fire at dusk, crash-landing into a rice paddy. He survived, but his co-pilot and two gunners died. He still recalls the sensation of the co-pilot's blood soaking through his flight glove—a sticky, warm texture he can feel even now, decades later. That specific texture, the fading light of dusk, and the distant thump of rotors instantly snap him back to the wreck. The memory feels alien, as though it belongs to some other man; yet the terror is vivid and immediate, flooding him without warning. He now avoids tactile sensations like damp fabric or certain lotions, and he arranges his schedule so he never lands a plane after 7 p.m.—the same time of day, every day.

The connection between triggers and his ongoing sense of threat is relentless. When Tama hears a helicopter overhead while driving to the airport, his heart hammers, and he finds himself scanning the sky for cover. Sudden movements by passengers or ground crew put him on guard; he has to consciously stop himself from ducking. At home, he keeps the blinds drawn after sunset and checks each room for exits before sitting down. He has come to believe the world is dangerous, and that belief makes the triggers feel like confirmations of danger. The noise of a passing helicopter is not just a sound—it means another attack could come. In turn, his hypervigilance amplifies his negative appraisals: if he is always on edge, there must be something wrong with him. He used to be a happy man, he says, but now he is always miserable, convinced he carries a permanent defect inside him.

The memory itself drives both threat and appraisals. When a sudden noise or texture brings the crash back without warning, the terror is so complete that Tama feels he is reliving it, which feeds his belief that the world is hostile. That belief, in turn, makes him more likely to notice threats—and more likely to misinterpret benign triggers as dangerous. At work, he avoids the crew lounge because of the rough fabric on the chairs, a texture that reminds him of the rice paddy mud. His co-pilot once joked that he was "jumpy," and Tama snapped, embarrassed; he now avoids that co-pilot on layovers. His wife has noticed he cannot sit through a movie with her because he fixates on the exit sign and begins to sweat when there is a helicopter scene. He tells her it's nothing, but he knows the memory is stealing his life.

What finally brought Tama to seek help was an incident last month. While taxiing his 737, the time-of-day alarm on his watch chimed at 7:02 p.m., and he froze, his hands locked on the yoke, until the tower called him twice. He was terrified he would lose his medical clearance. Now he sits in the therapist's office, hoping someone can stop the loop—the triggers that cue the memory, the memory that confirms the world is dangerous, the danger that makes him always watchful, and the watchfulness that brings the triggers back again. He is most afraid that the defective self he feels inside will eventually cost him the only thing he has left: the sky.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that the traumatic memory directly causes or increases triggers; instead, triggers cue the memory, and memory influences triggers only indirectly through appraisals.
The vignette does not convey that a sense of threat directly triggers or amplifies the trauma memory; threat leads to hypervigilance and triggers, but not directly to the memory.
